name: Vilcek Prizes for Creative Promise — Awards for Young Immigrant Scientists and Artists
description: The Vilcek Foundation awards Prizes for Creative Promise to young immigrant professionals who demonstrate outstanding early achievement in biomedical science, the arts, and culinary arts. Each prize is an unrestricted cash award of $50,000, enabling recipients to advance their work and careers. Applicants must be foreign-born and living in the United States. The program celebrates the contributions immigrants make to American society and aims to raise awareness of their impact across disciplines. Multiple prizes are awarded each year across different categories, including biomedical science, film, literature, and culinary arts. Recipients of DACA, permanent residents, naturalized citizens, and other visa holders are eligible.
eligibility: Foreign-born individuals living in the United States, aged 38 or younger at the time of nomination; must demonstrate exceptional early-career achievement in biomedical science, arts, or culinary arts; DACA recipients, permanent residents, and naturalized citizens are eligible
applicationProcess: Nominations open annually, typically in the fall. Candidates may be nominated by colleagues, mentors, or institutions. Self-nominations are also accepted. A panel of expert judges reviews nominations and selects winners. Visit vilcek.org for current cycle dates and nomination forms.
documentsRequired: Nomination form; curriculum vitae or resume; statement of accomplishments; evidence of immigration status (foreign-born, living in the US); letters of recommendation; portfolio or publication list as relevant to category

name: Golden Door Scholars — Full Tuition Scholarship for Undocumented and DACA Students
description: Golden Door Scholars provides full four-year college scholarships, career and fellowship support, mentorship, and community-building opportunities for undocumented students and DACA recipients in the United States. Selected scholars attend one of Golden Door Scholars' partner colleges and universities with tuition fully covered. Beyond financial support, the program offers professional development workshops, internship placements, and a strong alumni network. The organization was founded to address the gap in higher education access for students without legal immigration status who are ineligible for federal financial aid. Golden Door Scholars has helped hundreds of students access higher education and launch careers.
eligibility: Undocumented students and DACA/TPS recipients in the United States; must be high school seniors or current college students seeking to transfer; must demonstrate academic achievement and financial need; must plan to attend a Golden Door Scholars partner institution
amount: Full four-year tuition scholarship at partner colleges and universities
applicationProcess: Applications open annually, typically in the fall for students enrolling the following academic year. Applicants submit an online application with essays, transcripts, and financial information. Finalists are invited for interviews. Selected scholars are matched with partner institutions based on fit and availability.
geographicScope: United States — partner colleges and universities nationwide
documentsRequired: Online application form; high school or college transcripts; personal essays; proof of financial need; documentation of immigration status (undocumented, DACA, or TPS); letters of recommendation

name: Title III Part A — English Language Acquisition State Grants for Immigrant Students
description: Title III, Part A of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act provides formula grants to states for English language acquisition programs serving English learner (EL) and immigrant children and youth. States use their allotments to award subgrants to local educational agencies (LEAs) based on the number of EL and immigrant students enrolled. Funds support supplemental language instruction, professional development for teachers of ELs, and activities to help immigrant students integrate into U.S. schools. The program also includes a dedicated Immigrant Children and Youth subgrant for LEAs experiencing significant increases in immigrant student enrollment, providing additional resources for orientation services, academic support, and community engagement. This is one of the largest federal funding streams specifically designated for immigrant student education.
eligibility: English learner and immigrant children and youth enrolled in public K-12 schools in the United States; funds are distributed to state education agencies and then to local school districts based on enrollment data; individual students benefit through school programs, not direct applications
amount: Federal formula grant — approximately $890 million allocated annually; individual LEA subgrants vary based on EL student enrollment
applicationProcess: State education agencies apply to the U.S. Department of Education for annual formula grants. States then distribute subgrants to local educational agencies (school districts) based on EL and immigrant student counts. Individual families do not apply directly — benefits are delivered through school-based programs. Parents should contact their child's school or district to learn about available services.
geographicScope: United States — all 50 states, District of Columbia, and territories
documentsRequired: States submit consolidated applications to the U.S. Department of Education; LEAs apply to their state education agency; individual families need proof of school enrollment; no separate application required for students

name: Vilcek Foundation Grants for Immigrant-Serving Nonprofits
description: The Vilcek Foundation awards annual grants of up to $20,000 each to mission-driven nonprofit organizations that uplift immigrant communities and celebrate their contributions to American society. A total of $200,000 is distributed each year across multiple grantees. Eligible projects span the arts, sciences, education, social services, and community development. The program specifically targets organizations whose work advances the well-being, visibility, and integration of immigrant populations in the United States. Past grantees have included organizations providing legal services, arts education, workforce development, and health services to immigrant communities.
eligibility: 501(c)(3) nonprofit organizations in the United States whose mission directly supports immigrant communities; organizations must demonstrate measurable impact on immigrant populations through arts, sciences, education, or social services programming
amount: Up to $20,000 per organization; total annual pool of $200,000
applicationProcess: Applications open annually with a spring deadline (April 30 for 2026 cycle). Nonprofits submit an online application describing their mission, programs serving immigrants, and intended use of grant funds. A review committee evaluates applications based on impact, organizational capacity, and alignment with the Vilcek Foundation's mission. Recipients are announced in the fall.
documentsRequired: Online application form; proof of 501(c)(3) status; organizational budget; program description and impact metrics; most recent annual report or financial statements

name: First Literacy Grants — Adult Education and Literacy for Immigrants in Massachusetts
description: First Literacy supports community-based organizations in Massachusetts that provide adult basic education, English language learning, and literacy services to immigrants and refugees. Through its grant program, First Literacy funds innovative projects that help adult learners develop the reading, writing, math, and English language skills needed for employment, civic participation, and daily life. Grants support a range of activities including ESL classes, digital literacy training, workforce readiness programs, and family literacy initiatives. The organization partners with libraries, community organizations, and adult education centers to expand access to quality instruction for underserved populations, with particular emphasis on immigrant and refugee communities.
eligibility: Community-based organizations, libraries, and adult education programs in Massachusetts that serve adult learners, particularly immigrants and refugees; individual learners benefit through funded programs, not direct applications
amount: Grants vary by project — typically $5,000 to $25,000 per funded project
applicationProcess: Organizations apply directly to First Literacy through an annual grant cycle. Applications require a project description, budget, and evidence of serving immigrant or underserved adult learners. First Literacy staff review proposals and may conduct site visits. Individual learners should contact participating organizations for enrollment information.
geographicScope: Massachusetts — statewide, with concentration in Greater Boston area
documentsRequired: Grant application form; project proposal with timeline and budget; evidence of organizational capacity; data on target population served; proof of nonprofit or educational status
